papers.title_in_file: Robust and Efficient Single-Pixel Image Classification with Nonlinear Optics
papers.version_note: arXiv:2101.11696v1 preprint of an Optics Letters paper; the text layer of the figures is garbled, so figure values are named in anchors only where the body text repeats them.
papers.what_it_is: An experimental and simulated hybrid image classifier that uses partial Fourier transform, mode-selective sum-frequency upconversion, single-pixel power readings and a deep neural network to classify MNIST digits, including noisy ones.

assertions.value: The authors state that they study an approach where the upconversion is applied to images that undergo only a partial Fourier transform, realized by displacing the nonlinear crystal from the focal point of the Fourier lens.
quotes: Here, we study a new approach where the upconversion is applied to the images undergoing only partial Fourier transform.
it is easily realized in the current system by displacing the nonlinear crystal from the focal point of the Fourier lens for the images.
assertions.certainty_reason: The introduction states the scheme the paper studies (its own setup).

assertions.value: The authors state that in their previous system the mode-selective conversion is applied to fully Fourier-transformed images, which samples signature features in the Fourier domain but overlooks some identifying features in the original image domain.
quotes: In our previous system [30], the mode-selective conversion is applied to the fully Fourier-transformed images, which samples the signature features in the Fourier domain, but overlooks some important identifying features in the original image domain.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limitation of its own earlier system in the introduction.

assertions.value: The authors state that a Fourier lens of f = 200 mm focuses the coupled beam into a temperature-stabilized PPLN crystal for sum-frequency generation, and that the power readings of the sum-frequency generation are the features fed to a deep neural network for digit recognition.
quotes: A Fourier lens ( f =200 mm) is used to focus the coupled beam in a temperature-stabilized periodic poled lithium niobate (PPLN) crystal for sum-frequency (SF) generation process.
The power readings of the SF generation are extracted features from images, which are inputs to a deep neural network for digits recognition.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section on the experimental setup states it.

assertions.value: The authors state that they solve the coupled field equations (1)-(3) numerically with the standard split-step Fourier and adaptive step size methods, using a poling period of 19.36 micrometers for the PPLN.
quotes: We can use the standard split-step Fourier and
adaptive step size methods [37] to numerically solve Eqs.(1)-(3)
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its simulation method.

assertions.value: The authors state that they use a subset of the MNIST database made of the first 200 handwritten images of each digit, shuffled and separated into training (1600 images) and testing (400 images) sets, with the 28x28 images increased to 400x400 pixels.
quotes: A subset of the original database consisting of the ﬁrst 200 handwritten images of each digit is applied as our database.
training (1600 images) and testing (400 images) sets.
The resolution of these 28×28 images are increased to 400×400 pixels to match with the input signal beam size and SLM pitch.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the data set it tests on, which limits every accuracy it reports.
assertions.reader_inference: Only 400 test images are used, so a one-image change moves an accuracy by 0.25 percentage points.

assertions.value: The authors state that the deep neural network is the same as in their earlier work, a combination of one convolutional layer and five fully connected layers, trained with the ADAM gradient descent algorithm, with softmax at the output.
quotes: The structure of the deep neural network is same as the one in our previous work in [30]
which is a combination of one convolutional layer and ﬁve fully connected layers.
the adaptive moment estimation (ADAM) gradient descent algorithm is selected to minimize the loss between predictions and their ground truth.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section states the network.

assertions.value: The authors state that they follow the earlier work and use a set of 40 LG pump modes, and that they choose crystal displacements of 0, 27 mm and 40 mm because a larger displacement defocuses the light and suppresses sum-frequency generation.
quotes: Also, here we follow [30] to use a set of 40 LG modes, with l ∈ [−2, 2] and p ∈ [0, 7].
a large ∆ de-focuses the light and suppresses the SF generation.
we choose ∆ = 0, 27 mm and 40 mm in this study.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the mode set and displacements it tests.

assertions.value: The authors state that a larger crystal displacement may be accommodated by using a higher pump power to compensate for the loss of sum-frequency efficiency.
quotes: A larger ∆ may be accommodated by using a higher pump power to compensate for the SF efﬁciency loss.
assertions.certainty_reason: An untested statement by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the crystal at the Fourier plane the simulated accuracy is only 77.25% and the experimental accuracy is 81.25%, and attribute the difference likely to measurement errors in the upconverted sum-frequency power readings for high-order pump projection modes.
quotes: In this case, the simulated accuracy is only 77.25% and experimental accuracy is 81.25%.
This discrepancy is likely attributed to the measurement errors in the upconverted SF power readings for high-order pump projection modes.
assertions.certainty_reason: One experiment on 400 test images.

assertions.value: The authors report that with a crystal displacement of 27 mm both the simulated and experimental accuracy reached above 97%.
quotes: When the crystal is displaced by ∆ = 27 mm,
both the simulated and experimental accuracy reached above
97% as shown in Fig. 2(b) and (e), respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: One experiment on 400 test images.

assertions.value: The authors report that the accuracy can be further increased over 99% with a crystal displacement of 40 mm.
quotes: increased over 99% with ∆ = 40 mm.
assertions.certainty_reason: One experiment on 400 test images.

assertions.value: The authors report that, tested on MNIST handwritten digit images, a 40 mm crystal displacement increases the accuracy from 81.25% to 99.23%.
quotes: Tested on the MNIST (Modiﬁed National Institute of Standards and Technology) handwritten digit images, a 40 mm crystal displacement signiﬁcantly increases the accuracy from 81.25% to 99.23%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on a 400-image test set.
assertions.reader_inference: The 99.23% figure is for 400 test images drawn from the first 200 images of each digit, not the full MNIST test set.

assertions.value: The authors define the signal-to-noise ratio as 10 times the base-10 logarithm of the ratio of the variance of per-pixel phase values in the digit images to the variance of per-pixel phase values in the added noise masks.
quotes: SNR = 10 log10(σs2/σn2)
where σs2 and σn2 are the variance of per-pixel phase values in the digit images and the added noise masks
assertions.certainty_reason: Eq. (4) defines the SNR the paper's noise results use.

assertions.value: The authors report that the same technique enables robust pattern recognition with strong added noise, with an accuracy of about 83% even when the signal-to-noise ratio is as low as -17 dB.
quotes: The same technique enables robust pattern recognition when the images are mixed with strong noise, where a high accuracy ∼ 83% is achieved even when the signal-to-noise (SNR)
is as low as -17 dB.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that for noise-contaminated images both simulated and experimental results show better performance at a crystal displacement of 40 mm than at 27 mm, with an advantage that reaches 12.18% at an SNR of -15 dB.
quotes: both results reveal better performance with ∆ = 40 mm
than ∆ = 27 mm.
The advantage reaches 12.18% when the SNR
is -15 dB.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that at SNR of -15 dB and a displacement of 40 mm the simulated and experimental accuracies are 59% and 72.68%, and that halving the noise cluster size raises them to 91.25% in simulation and 93.4% in experiment.
quotes: The simulated and experimental results with SNR=-15 dB and ∆ = 40 mm in Fig. 3 (b) are 59% and 72.68%,
the accuracy increases to 91.25% and 93.4% in simulation and experiment, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that when the noise feature size is comparable with the image's characteristic features, it is difficult to distinguish them in both the original and Fourier domains.
quotes: When the noise feature size is comparable with the image’s characteristic features, it is difﬁcult to distinguish them in both original and Fourier domains.
assertions.certainty_reason: An explanation offered without a separate test.

assertions.value: The authors state that with partially Fourier-transformed images the signature features appear in the sum-frequency power of the first few LG modes, which removes the need to amplify the power of higher-order modes and allows normalization for each image, avoiding repeated per-mode normalization over the entire data set when new data are added.
quotes: This eliminates the need to amplify the SF power for higher-order modes, and allows normalization for each image.
avoiding the need of repeated normalization within each mode over the entire data set when new data are added.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument by the authors, not a separate measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that their previous method normalized the sum-frequency power by mode, which made the system prone to noise and fluctuations, and that adding new data requires renormalizing the whole data set and a new training process.
quotes: that method renders the system prone to noise and ﬂuctuations.
the whole data set needs to be normalized again and new training process is warranted for the best performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit of its previous method.

assertions.value: The authors report from simulation that 176 LG modes (l from -5 to 5, p from 0 to 15) raised the accuracy to 96% from 91%, while fewer modes lowered it from 87% (l from -2 to 2, p from 0 to 4) to 48% (l = 0, p from 0 to 4).
quotes: With 176 LG modes (l ∈ [−5, 5] and p ∈ [0, 15]), the accuracy improved to 96% from 91%.
the accuracy could drop quickly from 87% with l ∈ [−2, 2] and p ∈ [0, 4] to 48% with l = 0 and p ∈ [0, 4]).
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors report from simulation with the lowest order HG modes an accuracy of 88.5% at a displacement of 27 mm and 96.75% at 40 mm, both inferior to the simulated results with 40 LG modes, and conclude LG modes are more efficient and suitable for these digits.
quotes: 88.5% with ∆ = 27 mm and 96.75% with ∆ = 40 mm, which are all inferior to the simulated results with 40 LG modes in Fig. 2(b) and (c).
Therefore, LG modes are more efﬁcient and suitable for the feature extractions of the handwritten digits than
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated result from one study on one data set.

assertions.value: The authors state that in practice the optimum mode choice depends on the spatial characteristics of the target images.
quotes: shall depend on the spatial characteristics of the target images.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its LG over HG finding.

assertions.value: The authors state that LG mode bases performed better than HG mode bases, likely due to a lower cross-talk for the former.
quotes: showing better performance with the Laguerre Gaussian (LG) mode bases than the Hermite-Gaussian (HG) modes, likely due to a lower cross-talk for the former [34].
assertions.certainty_reason: A hedged explanation attributed to cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the robustness of this approach against strong noise invites future applications such as identifying occluded targets, widefield surveillance, and remote sensing under low visibility.
quotes: The robustness of this approach against strong noise invites its future applications in challenging tasks such as identifying occluded targets, wideﬁeld surveillance, and remote sensing under low visibility.
assertions.certainty_reason: A forward-looking statement without evidence in the paper.
